newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain to respect old HK assembly members--Cook.
newsitem.headline: Britain to respect old HK assembly members--Cook.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has said Britain will still give special status to members of Hong Kong's elected legislature even after China disbands it upon Monday night's handover.

Cook, in an interview with the Asian Wall Street Journal, also said he regretted Britain did not introduce democratic reforms in Hong Kong before it began discussions with China nearly two decades ago about returning the territory to China.
This would have been better than waiting until the handback was approaching. "Historians may be inclined to wonder whether that was the right way around," Cook told the Journal.
He said Britain considered it a duty to ensure China sticks to the 1984 treaty, the Joint Declaration, that sets out the terms of the sovereignty transfer at midnight on Monday.
But he ducked questions on the kind of pull that Britain could exert if China breaches the agreement.
"We're not the colonial power after June 30. We did not have direct powers of intervention in Hong Kong, nor should we," Cook said, adding that now was no time for "wild and dire threats".
But he noted that the international community, most recently the Denver, Colorado sumnit of eight industrialised democracies this month, has called for fresh legislative elections in Hong Kong.
The incoming government in the territory has offered to hold these elections by May, but Hong Kong's homegrown pro-democracy camp has sceptically called the offer a lie.

Britain and the United States are staging a ministerial boycott of the swearing-in ceremony for the new unelected Provisional Legislature hours after the handover, although they are still sending career diplomats along.

Underlining London's disapproval for the new body, Cook said Britain would accord visiting members of the doomed elected Legislative Council "the dignity and status and respect due" to them for the duration of the four year term for which they were elected in 1995.
In particular, Cook said, he would be very willing to meet Democratic Party leader Martin Lee, saying Lee was "plainly a politician with a considerable following in Hong Kong".
